tagline: Rural main streets and covered bridges on the roads toward Gettysburg
intro: Old Main Streets links rural towns between Emmitsburg and Mount Airy, with Thurmont at the foot of Catoctin Mountain. Covered bridges near Thurmont and Victorian residences in Uniontown give the drive its landmarks. Maryland's tourism office presents this state scenic byway as a journey through history, heritage and architecture. Its full itinerary covers 111 miles, with three to four hours of driving and two to three days suggested for exploring. The three covered bridges near Thurmont are Loy's Station, Roddy Road and Utica Mills.

These roads connected places that grew by serving travelers and trade. New Windsor developed at wagon-trail junctions, while Taneytown began as an agricultural trading center. During the Civil War, Union and Confederate soldiers used routes along this corridor to march north toward Gettysburg. Families and churches cared for the wounded.

For the upper loop, begin at Thurmont and head east through Detour, then Uniontown and Westminster. In Westminster, the Carroll Arts Center occupies a refurbished art-deco movie theater. From Westminster, the route turns northwest through Taneytown to Emmitsburg and returns south to Thurmont. A lower loop connects Uniontown with Union Bridge, Libertytown and New Windsor; a branch from Libertytown reaches Mount Airy through vineyard country.

moments.title: Detour
moments.text: Detour grew along the Western Maryland Railway. Its post office opened in 1905 and operated until 1993. The village lies just east of Double Pipe Creek, the Frederick County boundary, with Keymar to its east. Near Detour, Big Pipe Creek and Little Pipe Creek meet; their combined stream runs west for 1.6 miles to the Monocacy River.

moments.title: Taneytown
moments.text: George Washington described Taneytown as a small place, built along the street carrying the road, with buildings chiefly made of wood. Its position on the principal road between Gettysburg and Washington, D.C., later gave it a role in the Gettysburg campaign, although no combat occurred in town. Union General George Meade made his headquarters here for a period during the Civil War. Road and main street remain joined: Maryland Route 140 follows Baltimore Street through central Taneytown before continuing west toward Emmitsburg. The town’s history museum presents its past to residents and visitors.

moments.title: Emmitsburg
moments.text: Emmitsburg lost half its town to fire on the night of June 23, 1863. Union forces had fortified the town against the Confederate invasion. The battle instead took place twelve miles north at Gettysburg. Retreating Confederates briefly held Emmitsburg on July 4. At the National Shrine of St. Elizabeth Ann Seton, a monument recognizes another part of the town's history: the enslaved people who worked on the grounds from 1809 to 1865. The shrine honors the first American-born saint, and the town's Main Street includes buildings dating to the late 1700s.
